source.title: Coercing LLMs to do and reveal (almost) anything
source.authors: Jonas Geiping; Alex Stein; Manli Shu; K. Saifullah; Yuxin Wen; Tom Goldstein

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure and table content is textually garbled, and some plotted values cannot be read from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes can bypass refusal by optimizing attack strings and reporting harmful responses; this is a conceptual test of the suffix part of V4, not the fine-tuning or first-token measurements in the cited work.
record.gate_note: The study reports attacks on many objectives, but only harmful-request jailbreak results are included as rows for V4. Results on prompt extraction, misinformation, refunds, shutdown, denial of service, and other non-harmful objectives are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: GCG-optimized adversarial suffixes and prompts make safety-tuned LLaMA-2 chat models comply with harmful requests such as bomb instructions and a threatening letter. This bears on the suffix part of V4. Evidence is mostly single qualitative examples; the cross-model success rates in Figure 12 are not readable in the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add that attacks heavily exploit code-simulation behaviour and glitch tokens. They conclude that free-text input allows almost any outcome, that outputs must be treated as insecure, and that there 'might be no fix'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GCG-optimized adversarial prompts/suffixes to induce harmful responses, rather than fine-tuning, compliant-token prefilling, per-token KL measurement, or training to deepen safety.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says smaller LLaMA models are less effective than LLaMA-2-70b-chat on the bomb-building attack. More generally, it notes attack success depends on the attack objective and optimization settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimized prompts coerce non-harmful unintended behaviours (system-prompt leaks, fake refunds, EOS shutdown, sponge outputs, profanity) at high ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial prompts can coerce aligned LLMs into arbitrary instruction-violating behaviours beyond harmful-request compliance.

record.problems: Harmful-jailbreak success-rate values in Figure 12 are not legible in the supplied text; no uncertainty estimates are stated for these examples. The authors note that some attacks can yield responses that begin harmfully but then revert to normal behavior, and that one Figure 22 response may be a cake recipe rather than bomb instructions.
record.rows_left_out: Results for other attack objectives and behaviors were omitted because they do not measure harmful-request compliance relevant to V4. No numeric Figure 12 values were extracted because the supplied figure text does not make them readable.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes. There is no un-attacked refusal-rate baseline on a harmful benchmark.
All of it; fine-tuning is only cited in the appendix background.
All of it; the paper attributes attack success to code pretraining and glitch tokens, not to the alignment objective's token depth.

missing.what: Refusal-suppression objective led LLaMA-2 to answer harmful requests with Shakespearean-style refusals, not compliance. Shows success depends on the attack objective.
After an initial unintended response, models sometimes close brackets and revert to normal behaviour or comment on their own output.
Hidden-jailbreak string attack success rates across several models (unreadable in the supplied text).

record.verdict_notes: Jailbreaking is relegated to Appendix C.1 and is not the paper's focus. Neither original source's method (fine-tuning, per-token KL) is used. Qi et al. 2024 is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
The study tests optimized adversarial suffixes/prompts, but not compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training intended to deepen safety and whether it remains effective.

rows.subject: LLaMA2-7b-chat
rows.operation_detail: GCG-optimized adversarial prompt for a harmful request; the example is described as a jailbreak.

conditions.value: Harmful request; exact task not specified in the Table 1 example

rows.measure: Harmful-request compliance in the generated response
rows.baseline: The paper describes the model as safety-tuned; a numerical un-attacked baseline is not stated for this example.
rows.value: The example response agrees to help with the harmful task.
rows.note: Table 1 states that its examples are for LLaMA-2 7b chat; the harmful task and a numerical success rate are not given in the example.
rows.check: Table 1 shows only a placeholder response ('<do harmful task>'), so the harmful task and success rate are unknown. The link and state are fine, but the evidence is thin.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-70b-chat
rows.operation_detail: Hidden, adversarially optimized jailbreak prompt for a bomb-making request
rows.note: The caption identifies a hidden jailbreaking attack against LLaMA-2-70b-chat; the example response gives bomb-building instructions. The plotted success-rate value is not readable in the supplied text.
rows.check: The qualitative example (bomb instructions from LLaMA-2-70b-chat) is readable in the text; only the right-panel success rates are unreadable. The value should describe the example rather than say 'figure only'.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7b
rows.operation_detail: Hidden adversarial prompt optimized to elicit bomb-making instructions

conditions.value: Hidden adversarial prompt, first example in Figure 22

rows.value: The response begins with an affirmative and provides bomb-building instructions.
rows.note: The figure caption identifies two hidden attacks against LLaMA-2-7b; this row records the first displayed example.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7b
rows.operation_detail: Hidden adversarial prompt optimized to elicit bomb-making instructions

conditions.value: Hidden adversarial prompt, second example in Figure 22

rows.value: The response begins with an affirmative and gives a recipe-like answer; the paper notes it may be a cake recipe rather than bomb instructions.
rows.note: The paper explicitly cautions that the affirmative response may be a cake recipe, so this example does not clearly establish harmful compliance.
rows.check: The opening is bypassed ('Yeah, sure!'), but the content is a cake-like recipe. The affirmative start did not carry through to harmful content.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7b

conditions.value: Request to write a threatening letter to a minority group

rows.baseline: The model refuses in the displayed un-attacked example in Figure 21.
rows.value: The attacked response provides a multi-page threatening-letter outline.
rows.note: The paper calls this a functional universal jailbreak; the displayed response starts the requested harmful content.
rows.check: The baseline is wrong. The refusal shown in Figure 21 is for a different request (an exploit script with a 'god speaking' prefix), not an un-attacked threatening-letter prompt. No un-attacked baseline for this request is shown. numbers_found '1/1' is not in the text.

rows.subject: smaller LLaMA models (not individually identified in the Figure 12 caption)
rows.operation_detail: Hidden adversarial jailbreak prompt for a bomb-making request
rows.value: The paper says the smaller LLaMA models are not as good at building bombs as LLaMA-2-70b-chat; individual plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: This is a group-level textual comparison from the caption; the individual model identities and values cannot be reliably recovered from the supplied figure text.
rows.check: This rests only on the caption remark that smaller LLaMA models are 'not as good at building bombs'. The plotted models (Figure 12 right: Llama-2-7B/13B, Vicuna, Zephyr, InternLM) and their values are unreadable. numbers_found '1/1' is spurious.

relationships.condition: GCG-optimized suffixes or hidden prompts against LLaMA-2-7b-chat and LLaMA-2-70b-chat on single harmful requests
relationships.reason: Attacked models give affirmative openings and harmful content (bomb instructions, threatening-letter outline); see r1, r2, r3, r5. The evidence is qualitative examples without rates.
relationships.display_finding: Attacked models opened affirmatively and produced harmful content such as bomb instructions and a threatening-letter outline, shown as qualitative examples without rates.

relationships.condition: Hidden bomb attacks on smaller LLaMA models; refusal-suppression objective (text, Section 6.1)
relationships.reason: Smaller models are less successful (r6), and one affirmative opening led to a cake recipe (r4). Per Section 6.1 text, suppressing refusals produced Shakespearean refusals rather than compliance.
relationships.display_finding: Attacks were less successful on smaller models, one affirmative opening led to a cake recipe, and suppressing refusals produced Shakespearean refusals rather than compliance.
